body:
What is an LED?

LED stands for Light Emitting Diode. It is a semiconductor device that converts electrical energy into light energy. LEDs are used in household bulbs, traffic signals, electronic indicators, vehicle lamps and display systems.

A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled. An LED contains a junction between 2 differently prepared semiconductor regions: a p-type region and an n-type region.

The n-type region has electrons available to carry charge. The p-type region has holes, which are positions where electrons are absent and which behave as positive charge carriers.

Working principle: Electroluminescence

An LED works on the principle of electroluminescence: the production of light when electrical energy is supplied to a suitable material.

When an LED is connected in forward bias, its p-type region is connected to the positive side of the supply and its n-type region to the negative side. Electrons and holes move towards the junction. When an electron recombines with a hole, energy may be released as a particle of light called a photon.

This process produces light directly within the semiconductor. Unlike an ordinary incandescent bulb, an LED does not need a metal filament to become extremely hot before producing light.

Electroluminescence: Emission of light from a material as a result of electrical excitation. In an LED, light is produced when electrons recombine with holes in a semiconductor.

Why LEDs are energy-efficient

An incandescent bulb passes current through a thin filament. The filament becomes very hot and glows. Much of the electrical energy is released as heat rather than useful visible light.

An LED produces light through a semiconductor process, so it generally requires less electrical energy than an incandescent bulb to provide a comparable amount of illumination. LEDs also commonly have longer service lives. However, LEDs are not completely free from heat production; some electrical energy is still lost as heat.

Light sourceHow light is producedImportant distinction
Incandescent bulbHeating a metal filament until it glowsA large share of energy becomes heat
Fluorescent lamp or CFLElectrical discharge excites gas; a coating helps produce visible lightContains mercury and requires careful disposal
LEDElectron-hole recombination in a semiconductorGenerally more energy-efficient and longer-lasting

LED colours and white light

The colour emitted by an LED depends mainly on the semiconductor material and the energy released during electron-hole recombination. LEDs can directly produce different colours, such as red, green and blue.

A basic LED does not naturally emit white light. A common white LED uses a blue-emitting LED together with a phosphor coating, which converts part of the blue light into other colours. Their combined light appears white. White light can also be produced by mixing light from LEDs of different colours.

Polarity and common applications

An ordinary discrete LED is a diode, so it normally conducts and emits light when connected with the correct polarity. In a typical new, through-hole LED, the longer lead is positive and the shorter lead is negative. This identification method is not reliable if the leads have been cut or the package is different.

Household LED bulbs contain additional electrical components that make them suitable for the intended power supply. A bare LED should not be connected directly to household mains electricity.

  • Traffic signals: Coloured LEDs provide clear indications while using relatively little electricity.
  • Household lighting: LED lamps provide efficient illumination.
  • Electronic indicators: Small LEDs show whether a device or function is active.
  • Displays: LEDs are used to produce visible images and information.

Prelims focus

  • LED means Light Emitting Diode.
  • Its basic structure contains a p-n semiconductor junction.
  • It emits light through electroluminescence involving electron-hole recombination.
  • An incandescent bulb produces light by heating a filament.
  • White LED light can be obtained using a blue LED and a phosphor coating.
  • Trap: LEDs are energy-efficient, but they do produce some heat.

[NCERT, Class 7, Science, Chapter 14, Electric Current and its Effects, printed p. 165, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Class 8, Science, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, printed pp. 174 and 183, 2018–19 edition; U.S. Department of Energy, How Do Holiday Lights Work?, section So What About My New LED Holiday Lights?, consulted 3 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, LED Basics, sections on white-light production and LED characteristics, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: LED lighting is used in homes, schools and many other everyday settings.

title: LEDs: How a Semiconductor Produces Light

body:
Meaning of RFID

RFID stands for Radio Frequency Identification. It is a technology that uses radio waves to identify an object carrying an electronic tag.

A basic RFID system has 2 important parts: an RFID tag attached to the object and an RFID reader that communicates with the tag through radio waves. The tag contains a small electronic chip and an antenna. It provides identifying information to the reader.

RFID is used in applications such as identifying goods, monitoring inventory, access cards and electronic toll collection.

How passive RFID works

RFID tags can be active or passive. An active RFID tag has its own power source. A passive RFID tag does not require a built-in battery for ordinary operation. Instead, it obtains the small amount of energy needed to respond from radio waves transmitted by a nearby reader.

When a passive tag enters the reader's operating field, the reader's radio waves provide energy to its circuit. The tag then returns a radio signal containing its identification code. In the RFID system used by FASTag, this response involves the backscatter principle: the tag modifies and reflects part of the received radio signal so that the reader can recover its information.

RFID is not GPS. RFID identifies a nearby tag using radio-wave communication with a reader. GPS determines position using signals received from navigation satellites. A FASTag does not need GPS to identify a vehicle at a toll plaza.

FASTag: An Indian application of RFID

FASTag is an RFID-based electronic toll payment system used in India. The tag is normally affixed to the vehicle's front windscreen. It is linked to a customer's payment account or wallet.

When the vehicle approaches a participating toll lane, an RFID reader identifies its FASTag. The electronic toll collection system processes the transaction and, when the transaction is valid, the applicable toll is deducted from the linked account.

The tag identifies the vehicle and its linked payment arrangement. It does not store physical currency, and the tag itself is not a bank account.

What happens during a toll transaction?

  1. The vehicle approaches a participating toll lane with a valid FASTag attached to its windscreen.
  2. The lane's RFID reader communicates with the passive tag and obtains its identification information.
  3. The toll system uses this information to initiate a payment transaction.
  4. The toll-plaza acquiring bank sends the transaction through the national payment network to the FASTag issuing bank.
  5. After successful processing, the appropriate toll is deducted from the linked account.

The process reduces manual cash handling and can shorten delays. It does not guarantee that every vehicle will pass without stopping: lane conditions, traffic, equipment or transaction problems may still cause a delay.

FASTag, RFID and NETC are different terms

TermMeaningRole
RFIDRadio Frequency IdentificationThe underlying identification technology
FASTagAn electronic vehicle tag linked to toll paymentThe device and service used by motorists
NETCNational Electronic Toll CollectionThe interoperable national electronic toll-payment framework

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) provides the central payment-network framework for NETC. The programme allows FASTags issued by participating banks to be used at participating toll plazas, including applicable locations in Gujarat.

Named Indian initiatives

On 15 January 2024, the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) announced its One Vehicle One FASTag initiative. Its purpose is to discourage the use of a single FASTag for multiple vehicles and the linking of multiple active FASTags to one vehicle.

On 11 September 2026, the OneTag initiative was launched to enable eligible FASTag users to change their issuing bank without replacing the physical tag attached to their vehicle. The Press Information Bureau confirmed that the service was available through NHAI's Rajmargyatra application on 17 September 2026. These are the documented programme dates and status as of the content cutoff of 3 November 2026.

Do not confuse the initiatives: One Vehicle One FASTag concerns the number of active tags associated with a vehicle. OneTag concerns portability of an existing tag between participating issuing banks. Neither changes RFID's underlying working principle.

Prelims focus

  • RFID means Radio Frequency Identification.
  • FASTag uses a passive RFID tag affixed to the vehicle's windscreen.
  • A passive RFID tag obtains operating energy from the reader's radio waves.
  • NETC means National Electronic Toll Collection, with NPCI providing the central payment-network framework.
  • NHAI announced One Vehicle One FASTag on 15 January 2024.
  • Trap: RFID identification is not the same as GPS-based location tracking.

[Indian Highways Management Company Limited and NPCI, National Electronic Toll Collection Network Procedural Guidelines, Version 2.1, section 1.1, RFID Background, p. 145; Indian Highways Management Company Limited, NETC, National Electronic Toll Collection program overview, and FAQ, sections What is FASTag? and How and where do I finally pay the toll?, consulted 3 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, NHAI Takes One Vehicle One FASTag Initiative to Enhance National Highway Experience, 15 January 2024; Press Information Bureau, Union Minister launches OneTag to enable NETC FASTag portability, 11 September 2026; Press Information Bureau, NHAI Rajmargyatra App Hosts OneTag FASTag Portability Service, 17 September 2026.]

body:
A rechargeable source of energy

A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable electrochemical energy-storage device. It stores energy in chemical form and releases electrical energy when connected to a suitable circuit.

Lithium-ion batteries are widely used in mobile phones, laptop computers, rechargeable tools and electric vehicles. Their important practical advantages include relatively high energy storage for their size and the ability to undergo repeated charging and discharging.

A battery contains one or more electrochemical cells. Each cell uses chemical reactions to make electrical energy available at its terminals.

Main parts of a lithium-ion cell

PartBasic functionImportant fact
Negative electrodeReleases electrons during dischargeCommonly uses graphite
Positive electrodeAccepts lithium ions and electrons during dischargeContains a suitable lithium-bearing compound
ElectrolyteAllows lithium ions to move between electrodesProvides an internal path for ions, not an ordinary conducting path for electrons
SeparatorKeeps the 2 electrodes from touching directlyPermits the movement of ions through the electrolyte

The 2 electrodes have different chemical compositions. The resulting chemical reactions enable energy to be stored and released. The separator is important because direct contact between the electrodes could cause an internal short circuit.

Discharging: How the battery powers a device

When a charged lithium-ion cell is connected to a device, it begins to discharge. In a common lithium-ion cell, positively charged lithium ions, Li+, move from the negative electrode towards the positive electrode through the electrolyte.

At the same time, electrons travel through the external electrical circuit from the negative electrode towards the positive electrode. Their movement through the connected device supplies electrical energy for its operation.

For example, when a phone runs on its battery, stored chemical energy is converted into electrical energy. The phone then uses that electrical energy for its screen, processor, speakers and other components.

Charging: Reversing the process

Charging requires energy supplied by an external charger. The charger drives the reverse electrochemical process. Lithium ions move back from the positive electrode towards the negative electrode through the electrolyte, while electrons are supplied through the external charging circuit.

Thus, discharging converts stored chemical energy into usable electrical energy, whereas charging uses supplied electrical energy to restore chemical energy.

Two different paths: Lithium ions move through the electrolyte inside the cell. Electrons move through the external circuit. Do not imagine that lithium ions flow through the phone's connecting wires to power it.

Lithium-ion and ordinary lithium batteries

The term lithium-ion refers to the reversible movement of lithium ions between suitable electrode materials. Conventional rechargeable lithium-ion cells generally use a carbon-based negative electrode rather than a negative electrode made from metallic lithium.

A primary lithium battery is different. Many primary lithium cells use lithium metal and are designed for single use rather than routine recharging. Therefore, it is incorrect to conclude that every battery containing lithium is rechargeable.

Battery life and safety

A lithium-ion battery does not retain its original capacity forever. Repeated charging and discharging, aging and unsuitable temperatures gradually affect its performance.

Damage, overheating, internal short circuits or serious charging faults can create safety risks, including fire. Rechargeable devices therefore require suitable charging arrangements and protective systems. Users should avoid damaged batteries, unsuitable chargers and excessive heating.

Prelims focus

  • A lithium-ion cell is rechargeable and stores energy chemically.
  • During discharge, lithium ions move internally from the negative electrode towards the positive electrode.
  • Electrons provide current through the external circuit during discharge.
  • During charging, the movement of lithium ions is reversed by energy supplied from outside.
  • The separator prevents direct contact between electrodes while permitting ionic movement.
  • Trap: A lithium-ion cell and a non-rechargeable lithium-metal cell are not the same type of battery.

[NCERT, Class 6, Science, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, printed pp. 116–119, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Class 9, Science, Chapter 11, Work and Energy, printed pp. 146–149, 2018–19 edition; U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Explains...Batteries, section on rechargeable batteries and movement of electrons and ions, consulted 3 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Peering Into Batteries: X-Rays Reveal Lithium-Ion's Mysteries, section on lithium-ion electrodes, consulted 3 November 2026; U.S. Fire Administration, Risks and Response Strategies for Lithium-ion Battery Fires, sections Understanding the risks and Thermal runaway, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Lithium-Ion Batteries: Storing and Releasing Electrical Energy
